The town had a clock that never told the correct time. In winter it hurried; in summer it lagged. Every spring, someone proposed repairing it, and every autumn, the proposal disappeared beneath more urgent business: leaking roofs, school budgets, the question of whether the bakery could expand onto the pavement.

Only the watchmaker defended it. “Accuracy is common,” she said. “You can buy accuracy at the station. But this clock gives us something else.” Nobody asked what she meant, because she had a habit of answering simple questions with stories that lasted until the listener forgot why they had come.

One November morning, the clock stopped entirely. Its hands rested at twenty past four. Without its uneven chimes, the square seemed strangely larger. People crossed it quickly. The florist stopped putting a chair outside. Even the pigeons appeared to conduct their affairs with an unfamiliar and embarrassing sense of purpose.

The watchmaker climbed the tower carrying no tools. She sat beside the silent mechanism and opened the windows. Below, a child dropped an orange. It rolled between two strangers, who bent to catch it and knocked their heads together. Their laughter rose into the tower like something remembering its way.

That evening, the watchmaker repaired the clock. Not perfectly. She left it seven minutes slow. When asked why, she shrugged. “A town needs a little time that belongs to nobody.” And gradually, without discussing it, people began arriving early in the square, where there was nothing to do but wait.
